name: Ancient world trivia (easy)
description: 50 easy questions about prehistory and the early civilizations: Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus, China, the Americas. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: Which writing system, made of wedge-shaped marks, was developed by the Sumerians of Mesopotamia?
items.explain: Sumerian scribes created cuneiform, which used wedge-shaped impressions to record ideas and sounds. It is regarded as the first system of writing.

items.question: Ancient Mesopotamia lay between which two rivers?
items.explain: The name Mesopotamia refers to the region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in southwestern Asia.

items.question: Sumer, the site of the earliest known civilization, lay in what is now southern part of which modern country?
items.explain: Sumer was in southern Mesopotamia, in the area that is now southern Iraq.

items.question: Hammurabi, famous for his set of laws, was the best-known king of which ancient city?
items.explain: Hammurabi was the sixth ruler of the first dynasty of Babylon, reigning around 1792–1750 BCE.

items.question: The Code of Hammurabi is famous for which principle of retributive justice?
items.explain: The code is known for prescribing retributive justice for bodily injuries, which is summed up as 'an eye for an eye'.

items.question: Because some of the earliest civilizations arose there, Mesopotamia is often given which nickname?
answers: The Land of the Rising Sun
items.explain: Mesopotamia is widely described as one of the earliest cradles of civilization.

items.question: For which pharaoh was the Great Pyramid of Giza built as a royal tomb?
items.explain: The Great Pyramid was built as the tomb of Khufu (also called Cheops), the second king of Egypt's 4th dynasty.

items.question: The Pyramids of Giza stand on the west bank of which river?
items.explain: The Great Pyramid and its neighbours are on the west bank of the Nile in northern Egypt.

items.question: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World is the only one still standing today?
items.explain: The Great Pyramid at Giza is the only ancient wonder that survives.

source.title: What We Really Know About the Great Pyramid of Giza & Its Builder

items.question: According to archaeological evidence, who mainly built the Egyptian pyramids?
items.explain: Archaeology suggests the pyramids were built by free, professional builders, not by the mass of slaves described in later legends.

source.title: What We Really Know About the Great Pyramid of Giza & Its Builder

items.question: The Rosetta Stone became the key to deciphering which ancient script?
items.explain: The same decree is inscribed in three scripts, and scholars could still read the Greek. That let them decode the hieroglyphs.

items.question: Besides hieroglyphs and Demotic, which language is inscribed on the Rosetta Stone?
items.explain: The stone carries one decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic script and ancient Greek.

items.question: Which French scholar realized that hieroglyphs recorded the sounds of the Egyptian language, helping to decode them?
items.explain: Champollion showed that hieroglyphs recorded the sounds of the Egyptian language, which laid the foundations of modern Egyptology.

items.question: Which British archaeologist discovered the tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922?
items.explain: Howard Carter found the largely intact tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922.

items.question: In which famous Egyptian burial ground was Tutankhamun's tomb found?
items.explain: Carter's workmen found the steps to the tomb in the Valley of the Kings on 4 November 1922.

source.title: Entrance to King Tut's tomb discovered

items.question: Which iconic piece of ancient Egyptian art, made of solid gold, adorned Tutankhamun's mummy?
items.explain: The solid-gold funerary mask that covered the king's mummy is among the most iconic works of Egyptian art ever found.

source.title: Tutankhamun's Tomb: The Thrill of Discovery - The Metropolitan Museum of Art

items.question: Which natural salt did ancient Egyptian embalmers use to dry out bodies during mummification?
items.explain: Egyptian embalmers used natron, a salt found naturally in Egypt, to dry the body.

source.title: How to mummify a pharaoh: A step-by-step guide - History Skills

items.question: During mummification, which organ did embalmers remove with a hook and then discard?
items.explain: Priests removed the brain with a brain hook and threw it away. The heart was kept because it was thought to be the seat of a person's spirit.

items.question: Which two cities were the greatest urban centers of the Indus Valley Civilization?
items.explain: The Indus civilization is known for two large cities, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, plus more than 100 towns and villages.

items.question: In which modern country are the ruins of Mohenjo-daro found?
items.explain: Mohenjo-daro is in the Sindh province of present-day Pakistan, on the Indus River.

items.question: Which other name is used for the Indus Valley Civilization?
items.explain: The civilization is also called Harappan, after Harappa, one of its two great cities.

items.question: Indus cities such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are celebrated for early examples of what?
items.explain: These cities had grid-based street layouts, standardized bricks and extensive drainage systems.

source.title: Indus Valley Civilization - World History Encyclopedia

items.question: For which ruler was the famous Terracotta Army created?
items.explain: The Terracotta Army guards the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first unifier of China.

source.title: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

items.question: Who discovered the Terracotta Army in 1974?
items.explain: The army was found on 29 March 1974 by farmers who were digging a well near Xi'an.

items.question: Near which Chinese city is the Terracotta Army located?
items.explain: The army lies in Lintong District, Xi'an, in Shaanxi province.

items.question: Which dynasty's first emperor joined earlier fortifications into a single northern defense, creating the first Great Wall?
items.explain: Around 220 BCE, Qin Shi Huang connected sections of earlier walls into a united defense against invasions from the north.

items.question: Most of the Great Wall of China that survives and is visible today was built by which dynasty?
items.explain: The wall seen today is almost entirely the work of the Ming dynasty, which added the distinctive watchtowers.

source.title: Great Wall of China - World History Encyclopedia

items.question: Who supplied most of the labor for the Great Wall built under Qin Shi Huang?
items.explain: The Qin-era wall was built largely by soldiers, conscripts and convicts sent north under guard.

source.title: Great Wall of China - World History Encyclopedia

items.question: In 221 BCE, Qin Shi Huang became the first ruler to do what?
items.explain: Qin Shi Huang proclaimed himself first emperor of China in 221 BCE after conquering the rival states.

source.title: What You Need to Know About China's Terra-Cotta Warriors and the First Qin Emperor

items.question: Which ancient civilization built the city of Chichen Itza on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula?
items.explain: Chichen Itza was a Maya city, later influenced by the Toltec civilization.

items.question: What is the most famous structure at Chichen Itza called?
items.explain: The Temple of Kukulcán, also known as El Castillo, is the best-known building at Chichen Itza.

items.question: The name Chichen Itza is linked to a large natural sinkhole where the Maya threw offerings. What is such a sinkhole called?
items.explain: The name probably comes from the Sacred Cenote, a large sinkhole into which the Maya threw offerings of jade and gold.

items.question: Which trio of crops was central to early Maya agriculture?
items.explain: The early Maya were farmers who grew crops such as corn, beans, squash and cassava.

items.question: Which modern capital city was built over the ruins of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan?
items.explain: Tenochtitlan stood on the site of modern Mexico City, in the marshes of Lake Texcoco.

items.question: According to legend, what sign told the Aztecs where to found Tenochtitlan?
answers: A jaguar standing on a rock devouring a deer
An eagle perched on a cactus eating a snake
A hummingbird hovering above a golden lake
A serpent coiled around a temple stairway
items.correct: An eagle perched on a cactus eating a snake
items.explain: The god Huitzilopochtli told the Mexica to build where they saw an eagle on a cactus eating a snake.

items.question: Which Spanish conquistador led the campaign that destroyed the Aztec capital in 1521?
items.explain: Tenochtitlan was destroyed by the Spanish under Hernán Cortés in 1521.

items.question: What did the Aztecs use as a form of money?
items.explain: Aztec people used cocoa beans as money.

items.question: In which modern country is the Inca site of Machu Picchu?
items.explain: Machu Picchu is in the Andes of Peru, about 50 miles northwest of Cuzco.

items.question: Which city was the capital of the Inca Empire?
items.explain: Cuzco (Cusco) was the capital of the Inca Empire, known as Tawantinsuyu.

items.question: How were the stones in Inca masonry at Machu Picchu fitted together?
answers: Cut to fit tightly without mortar
items.correct: Cut to fit tightly without mortar
items.explain: Machu Picchu's buildings show Inca masonry, with stones cut to fit together without mortar.

items.question: What kind of surgery does evidence show that the Inca performed?
items.explain: Evidence shows that the Inca performed brain surgeries.

items.question: In which country is the Lascaux cave, famous for its prehistoric paintings?
items.explain: Lascaux is in southwestern France, near Montignac in the Dordogne region.

items.question: Who discovered the Lascaux cave paintings in 1940?
items.explain: Four teenagers stumbled on the paintings after following their dog down a narrow entrance into the cavern.

items.question: Roughly how old are the Lascaux cave paintings?
items.explain: The animal paintings at Lascaux are about 15,000 to 17,000 years old, from the Upper Paleolithic period.

items.question: What major change defines the Neolithic Revolution?
answers: A shift from farming to factory production
A move from cities back to nomadic herding
A switch from stone tools to iron tools
A shift from hunting and gathering to farming and settlement
items.correct: A shift from hunting and gathering to farming and settlement
items.explain: During the Neolithic Revolution, humans began cultivating plants, breeding animals for food and forming permanent settlements.

items.question: Roughly how long ago did the Neolithic Revolution begin?
items.explain: The shift from nomadic hunting and gathering to settled farming began around 12,000 years ago.

items.question: Which crop became a staple for early farmers in the Middle East, thanks to its huge natural stands there?
items.explain: Early Middle Eastern farmers relied on the abundant natural stands of wheat and barley. Rice, maize and sorghum became staples in other regions.

source.title: Dynamics of the Neolithic Revolution - World History Encyclopedia

items.question: The Neolithic period is also known by what name?
items.explain: The Neolithic is also called the New Stone Age, a period marked by farming and permanent settlements.

items.question: In which English county does the prehistoric monument Stonehenge stand?
items.explain: Stonehenge is a prehistoric monument in Wiltshire, England, and part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

items.question: Roughly how long ago did work on Stonehenge begin?
items.explain: Work began on Stonehenge about 5,000 years ago, and it was built in stages over many years.
